title: Chain of custody of seized contraband - a common defence ground
p1:
A seizure alone does not always win a case.

What happens to the seized material after it is taken into custody can become the turning point.
p2: Many people assume that once contraband is recovered, the evidence is automatically reliable. But the law also looks at whether the evidence was properly handled, stored, documented, and produced through every stage.
p3:
This process is called the chain of custody. It is the record showing who handled the seized material, when it was transferred, and whether it remained protected from tampering or mistakes.

A gap in this chain can raise doubts about the authenticity of the evidence. That is why defence teams often examine seizure records, storage details, and laboratory procedures closely.

A strong case is not only about what was found, but also about how it was preserved.
